newsitem.title: Mongolia: Mongolians vote for president, tight race expected.
newsitem.headline: Mongolians vote for president, tight race expected.

text.p: Mongolians rode and walked to the polls on Sunday to vote for a new president in what is expected to be a neck-and-neck race between the nation's reformist leader and his ex-communist challenger.
With five hours to go before polls closed at 10.00 p.m. (1300 GMT), over half of the 1.1 million eligible voters had cast their ballots, election officials told Reuters.
But officials in outlying districts of the capital later said that turnout was running at well over 70 percent.
Some voters arrived on horseback while others walked from their felt tents on the outskirts of the capital to reach polling stations.

In a military hospital in the capital a group of election officials collected ballots from bed-ridden patients. Those not too sick to walk shuffled to vote in a room normally used for medical examinations.
A smiling President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat cast his ballot early and told his electorate this was a crucial contest for the formerly communist nation.
"This is an important election," said the 55-year-old candidate of the Democratic Union Coalition as he and his wife Tsevelmaa greeted voters at a polling station in the capital.
"Whoever is elected will lead us into the next century."

Ochirbat, who won Mongolia's first direct presidential election in June 1993 as an opposition candidate after he was dumped by the then-ruling party, the ex-communist Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party, has promised to continue his drive for democracy if given another four-year term.
He has also pledged to eradicate poverty in a country where at least one in five people live below the official poverty line with an income of $10 a month.

His main opponent, Natsagiin Bagabandi of the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party that had ruled for 75 years before their shock defeat last year, has campaigned for a slowdown of reforms that have created widespread economic dislocation.
Bagabandi, 47, has tried to appeal to those who have been left jobless as Mongolia moves from Stalinist central planning to a market economy.
"If I become president...I will direct my efforts to make the state work like a real state," he said as he cast his vote.
A poll by the Sant Maaral Centre, a local think tank, gave the challenger 51 percent of the vote to the president's 44 percent.
Ochirbat's party controls parliament but the challenger, if elected, might be able to block legislation with a veto.
Officials of both of the two main parties voiced confidence that their candidate would emerge victorious.

Voters in this vast land wedged between Russia and China have a third candidate to choose from, Jambiin Gombojav, a parliament member running on the Mongolian Traditional United Party ticket. He is far behind the front-runners.
Results from across the sprawling land of the steppes were expected to be known on Monday at the earliest.
